pages.text: Far in the north, the summer was ending. The mornings were cool now, and the frogs in the marsh were quiet. On a big rooftop nest stood Long-Legs, a young stork only three months old. All around him, storks were gathering. They circled over the fields, clattering their beaks.
pages.speech: Far in the north, the summer was ending. The mornings were cool now, and the frogs in the marsh were quiet. On a big rooftop nest stood Long-Legs, a young stork only three months old. All around him, storks were gathering. They circled over the fields, clattering their beaks.

pages.text: “Why must we go?” Long-Legs asked a big stork beside him. “I like it here.” The big stork clattered her beak. “Soon the cold will come,” she said. “The frogs will hide, and the fields will be bare. Where we are going, there will be food.”
pages.speech: “Why must we go?” Long-Legs asked a big stork beside him. “I like it here.” The big stork clattered her beak. “Soon the cold will come,” she said. “The frogs will hide, and the fields will be bare. Where we are going, there will be food.”

pages.text: Long-Legs flapped his wings as hard as he could. Flap, flap, flap. He rose a little, then sank down again, puffing. “I can’t flap all the way,” he said. “It’s too far.” “Nobody flaps all the way,” said the big stork. “Wait for the sun.”
pages.speech: Long-Legs flapped his wings as hard as he could. Flap, flap, flap. He rose a little, then sank down again, puffing. “I can’t flap all the way,” he said. “It’s too far.” “Nobody flaps all the way,” said the big stork. “Wait for the sun.”

pages.text: So the next morning, the storks waited. Nobody flew while the ground was cold. Then the sun climbed higher and warmed the fields. Over the warm ground, the air began to rise, slowly, like an invisible tower. Nobody could see it. But the storks could feel it.
pages.speech: So the next morning, the storks waited. Nobody flew while the ground was cold. Then the sun climbed higher and warmed the fields. Over the warm ground, the air began to rise, slowly, like an invisible tower. Nobody could see it. But the storks could feel it.

pages.text: “Now!” said the big stork. She opened her wide wings and stepped into the rising air. Up she went, round and round, without a single flap. Long-Legs opened his wings too. The warm air lifted him like a hand. Round and round, and up and up.
pages.speech: “Now!” said the big stork. She opened her wide wings and stepped into the rising air. Up she went, round and round, without a single flap. Long-Legs opened his wings too. The warm air lifted him like a hand. Round and round, and up and up.

pages.text: At the top, the storks were tiny specks in the sky. Then they stretched out their necks and glided south. Down and down they slid, a long, long way. At last they found the next warm tower. Round and round, and up and up again. Flying was easy, if you knew where the warm air was.
pages.speech: At the top, the storks were tiny specks in the sky. Then they stretched out their necks and glided south. Down and down they slid, a long, long way. At last they found the next warm tower. Round and round, and up and up again. Flying was easy, if you knew where the warm air was.

pages.text: One day, they came to the edge of the sea. The water shone blue and flat, all the way to the sky. “Let’s fly straight across,” said Long-Legs. “It’s shorter.” The big stork shook her head. “No warm air rises over the sea,” she said. “We follow the land.” So the flock turned and flew along the shore.

The water shone blue and flat, all the way to the sky. “Let’s fly straight across,” said Long-Legs. “It’s shorter.” The big stork shook her head. “No warm air rises over the sea,” she said. “We follow the land.” So the flock turned and flew along the shore.

pages.text: Every evening, when the air grew cool, the storks came down to rest. They stood in fields and in tall trees, one leg tucked up, beaks resting on their chests. Long-Legs was tired right down to his feathers. Above him, the stars came out. Tomorrow there would be more sky.
pages.speech: Every evening, when the air grew cool, the storks came down to rest. They stood in fields and in tall trees, one leg tucked up, beaks resting on their chests. Long-Legs was tired right down to his feathers. Above him, the stars came out. Tomorrow there would be more sky.

pages.text: Day after day they flew, and the land below them changed. First there were dark forests and rivers. Then came brown hills, dry fields and small white houses. The days grew warm again. Long-Legs’ wings grew stronger, and he stopped puffing.
pages.speech: Day after day they flew, and the land below them changed. First there were dark forests and rivers. Then came brown hills, dry fields and small white houses. The days grew warm again. Long-Legs’ wings grew stronger, and he stopped puffing.

pages.text: One afternoon they saw a green valley, full of shining fishponds. “Down!” called the big stork. Thousands of storks spiralled down together, like a great white whirl. They landed by the water, and they ate and ate. Long-Legs had never seen so many storks in one place.
pages.speech: One afternoon they saw a green valley, full of shining fishponds. “Down!” called the big stork. Thousands of storks spiralled down together, like a great white whirl. They landed by the water, and they ate and ate. Long-Legs had never seen so many storks in one place.

pages.text: On a hill above the valley sat a girl and her grandfather. The girl held the binoculars, and her grandfather held a notebook. “There are so many!” she said. “How can we ever count them?” “In fives,” said her grandfather. He drew four little lines and one line across them. “Five. Now you try.”
pages.speech: On a hill above the valley sat a girl and her grandfather. The girl held the binoculars, and her grandfather held a notebook. “There are so many!” she said. “How can we ever count them?” “In fives,” said her grandfather. He drew four little lines and one line across them. “Five. Now you try.”

pages.text: The girl counted and drew, counted and drew. Four lines and one across, four lines and one across. Her page filled up with little gates. Down by a pond, a young stork stood on one leg and looked up at the hill. The girl lowered her binoculars and waved.
pages.speech: The girl counted and drew, counted and drew. Four lines and one across, four lines and one across. Her page filled up with little gates. Down by a pond, a young stork stood on one leg and looked up at the hill. The girl lowered her binoculars and waved.

pages.text: In the morning, the valley was cool and misty. The storks waited. Then the sun warmed the ground, and the air began to rise. This time, Long-Legs felt it first. He opened his wings and stepped in. Round and round, and up and up, and the other storks rose behind him.
pages.speech: In the morning, the valley was cool and misty. The storks waited. Then the sun warmed the ground, and the air began to rise. This time, Long-Legs felt it first. He opened his wings and stepped in. Round and round, and up and up, and the other storks rose behind him.

pages.text: Up on the hill, the girl watched the storks turn into a slow white tower. Then the tower drifted south and was gone. “Will they come back?” she asked. “In spring,” said her grandfather. “Storks fly back north the same way.” The girl drew one more stork in her notebook. One spring, Long-Legs would come back too.

activity.title: Sky Tally
activity.goal: Count with tally marks while watching nature.

steps.caption: Draw three columns: small, medium, big. Guess which wins.
One line for each bird. Every fifth goes across.
Which column won? Was your guess right?

activity.safety: Sit in the shade at a cool time of day, with a hat and water. Never look straight at the sun. Watch the birds; do not touch or feed them. If there is an accident, call your local emergency number.
activity.forAdult: In the story, Long-Legs learns why storks leave the north when the cold comes, and how they make such a long journey. White storks do not flap all the way. They wait until the sun has warmed the ground, ride the warm air that rises from it in slow circles, then glide to the next rising column. No such warm air forms over the open sea, so they follow the land, and they fly only by day. In autumn, from about August, huge numbers pass over Israel, and green valleys with fishponds are important resting places. Young storks can make their first journey without their parents. This activity turns the girl’s counting on the hill into a real watch. Choose a cool time of day (in hot months, before ten in the morning or after four in the afternoon), sit in the shade with hats and water, and watch the sky for about fifteen minutes. Before you start, the child draws three columns for small, medium and big birds and guesses which will win. Each bird that flies past gets one line in its column. Every fifth line goes across the other four, making a “gate”. At the end, count the gates in fives (five, ten, fifteen) and then the lines left over. Was the guess right? Praise careful watching and steady counting (“you didn’t miss one”). To make it easier, use one column only. To make it harder, add a column for birds flying in a group, or watch again on another day and compare.
activity.inClass: Groups of four sit together outside, in the shade. Each child watches one part of the sky (towards the building, the trees, the road, the open sky) and keeps their own tally. At the end, the group adds its four tallies together, counting the gates in fives, and the class compares groups.
